entries.727fbe875de79bbc1e1cf508d383011131fab314: <div sID="gen6968" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="20" osisID="1Kgs.20" sID="1Kgs.20"/> <div eID="gen6968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6969" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen6970" type="x-p"/> This chapter is the history of a war between Ben-hadad king of Syria and Ahab king of Israel, in which Ahab was, once and again, victorious. We read nothing of Elijah or Elishain all this story; Jezebel's rage, it is probable, had abated, and the persecution of the prophets began to cool, which gleam of peace Elijah improved. He appeared not at court, but, being told how many thousands of good people there were in Israel more than he thought of, employed himself, as we may suppose, in founding religious houses, schools, or colleges of prophets, in several parts of the country, to be nurseries of religion, that they might help to reform the nation when the throne and court would not be reformed. While he was thus busied, God favoured the nation with the successes we here read of, which were the more remarkable because obtained against Ben-hadad king of Syria, whose successor, Hazael, was ordained to be a scourge to Israel. They must shortly suffer by the Syrians, and yet now triumphed over them, that, if possible, they might be led to repentance by the goodness of God. Here is, I. Ben-hadad's descent upon Israel, and his insolent demand, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.1-1Kgs.20.11">ver. 1-11</reference>. II. The defeat Ahab gave him, encouraged and directed by a prophet, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.12-1Kgs.20.21">ver. 12-21</reference>. III. The Syrians rallying again, and the second defeat Ahab gave them, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.22-1Kgs.20.30">ver. 22-30</reference>. IV. The covenant of peace Ahab made with Ben-hadad, when he had him at his mercy (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.31-1Kgs.20.34">ver. 31-34</reference>), for which he is reproved and threatened by a prophet, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.35-1Kgs.20.43">ver. 35-43</reference>.
entries.dd016093c459a318d9865a964190a97a14830d9a: <div eID="gen6970" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen6969" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Ben-hadad's Insolent Demand. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 900.)</title> <div sID="gen6971" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And Benhadad the king of Syria gathered all his host together: and <hi type="italic">there were</hi> thirty and two kings with him, and horses, and chariots: and he went up and besieged Samaria, and warred against it. <hi type="super">2</hi> And he sent messengers to Ahab king of Israel into the city, and said unto him, Thus saith Benhadad, <hi type="super">3</hi> Thy silver and thy gold <hi type="italic">is</hi> mine; thy wives also and thy children, <hi type="italic">even</hi> the goodliest, <hi type="italic">are</hi> mine. <hi type="super">4</hi> And the king of Israel answered and said, My lord, O king, according to thy saying, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> thine, and all that I have. <hi type="super">5</hi> And the messengers came again, and said, Thus speaketh Benhadad, saying, Although I have sent unto thee, saying, Thou shalt deliver me thy silver, and thy gold, and thy wives, and thy children; <hi type="super">6</hi> Yet I will send my servants unto thee to morrow about this time, and they shall search thine house, and the houses of thy servants; and it shall be, <hi type="italic">that</hi> whatsoever is pleasant in thine eyes, they shall put <hi type="italic">it</hi> in their hand, and take <hi type="italic">it</hi> away. <hi type="super">7</hi> Then the king of Israel called all the elders of the land, and said, Mark, I pray you, and see how this <hi type="italic">man</hi> seeketh mischief: for he sent unto me for my wives, and for my children, and for my silver, and for my gold; and I denied him not. <hi type="super">8</hi> And all the elders and all the people said unto him, Hearken not <hi type="italic">unto him,</hi> nor consent. <hi type="super">9</hi> Wherefore he said unto the messengers of Benhadad, Tell my lord the king, All that thou didst send for to thy servant at the first I will do: but this thing I may not do. And the messengers departed, and brought him word again. <hi type="super">10</hi> And Benhadad sent unto him, and said, The gods do so unto me, and more also, if the dust of Samaria shall suffice for handfuls for all the people that follow me. <hi type="super">11</hi> And the king of Israel answered and said, Tell <hi type="italic">him,</hi> Let not him that girdeth on <hi type="italic">his harness</hi> boast himself as he that putteth it off. <div eID="gen6971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6972" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The threatening descent which Ben-hadad made upon Ahab's kingdom, and the siege he laid to Samaria, his royal city, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.1">v. 1</reference>. What the ground of the quarrel was we are not told; covetousness and ambition were the principle, which would never want some pretence or other. David in his time had quite subdued the Syrians and made them tributaries to Israel, but Israel's apostasy from God makes them formidable again. Asa had tempted the Syrians to invade Israel once (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.18-1Kgs.15.20">ch. xv. 18-20</reference>), and now they did it of their own accord. It is dangerous bringing a foreign force into the country: posterity may pay dearly for it. Ben-hadad had with him thirty-two kings, who were either tributaries to him, and bound in duty to attend him, or confederates with him, and bound in interest to assist him. How little did the title of king look when all these poor petty governors pretended to it! <div eID="gen6972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6973" type="x-p"/> II. The treaty between these two kings. Surely Israel's defence had departed from them, or else the Syrians could not have marched so readily, and with so little opposition, to Samaria, the head and heart of the country, a city lately built, and therefore, we may suppose, not well fortified, but likely to fall quickly into the hands of the invaders; both sides are aware of this, and therefore, <div eID="gen6973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6974" type="x-p"/> 1. Ben-hadad's proud spirit sends Ahab a very insolent demand, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.2-1Kgs.20.3">v. 2, 3</reference>. A parley is sounded, and a trumpeter (we may suppose) is sent into the city, to let Ahab know that he will raise the siege upon condition that Ahab become his vassal (Nay, his <hi type="italic">villain</hi>), and not only pay him a tribute out of what he has, but make over his title to Ben-hadad, and hold all at his will, even his wives and children, the godliest of them. The manner of expression is designed to gall them; "All shall be mine, without exception." <div eID="gen6974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6975" type="x-p"/> 2. Ahab's poor spirit sends Ben-hadad a very disgraceful submission. It is general indeed (he cannot mention particulars in his surrender with so much pleasure as Ben-hadad did in his demand), but it is effectual: <hi type="italic">I am thine, and all that I have,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.4">v. 4</reference>. See the effect of sin. (1.) If he had not by sin provoked God to depart from him, Ben-hadad could not have made such a demand. Sin brings men into such straits, by putting them out of divine protection. If God may not rule us, our enemies shall. A rebel to God is a slave to all besides. Ahab had prepared his silver and gold for Baal, <reference osisRef="Hos.2.8">Hos. ii. 8</reference>. Justly therefore is it taken from him; such an alienating amounts to a forfeiture. (2.) If he had not by sin wronged his own conscience, and set that against him, he could not have made such a mean surrender. Guilt dispirits men, and makes them cowards. He knew Baal could not help, and had no reason to think that God would, and therefore was content to buy his life upon any terms. Skin for skin, and all that is dear to him, he will give for it; he will rather live a beggar than not die a prince. <div eID="gen6975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6976" type="x-p"/> 3. Ben-hadad's proud spirit rises upon his submission, and becomes yet more insolent and imperious, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.5-1Kgs.20.6">v. 5, 6</reference>. Ahab had laid his all at his feet, at his mercy, expecting that one king would use another generously, that this acknowledgment of Ben-hadad's sovereignty would content him, the honour was sufficient for the present, and he might hereafter make use of it if he saw cause (<hi type="italic">Satis est prostrasse leoni</hi>—<hi type="italic">It suffices the lion to have laid his victim prostrate</hi>); but this will not serve. (1.) Ben-hadad is as covetous as he is proud, and cannot go away unless he have the possession as well as the dominion. He thinks it not enough to call it his, unless he have it in his hands. He will not so much as lend Ahab the use of his own goods above a day longer. (2.) He is as spiteful as he is haughty. Had he come himself to select what he had a mind for, it would have shown some respect to a crowned head; but he will send his servants to insult the prince, and hector over him, to rifle the palace, and strip it of all its ornaments; nay, to give Ahab the more vexation, they shall be ordered, not only to take what they please, but, if they can learn which are the persons or things that Ahab is in a particular manner fond of, to take those: <hi type="italic">Whatsoever is pleasant in thy eyes they shall take away.</hi> We are often crossed in that which we most dote upon; and that proves least safe which is most dear. (3.) He is as unreasonable as he is unjust, and will construe the surrender Ahab made for himself as made for all his subjects too, and will have them also to lie at his mercy: "They shall search, not only thy house, but <hi type="italic">the houses of thy servants</hi> too, and plunder them at discretion." Blessed be God for peace and property, and that what we have we can call our own. <div eID="gen6976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6977" type="x-p"/> 4. Ahab's poor spirit begins to rise too, upon this growing insolence; and, if it becomes not bold, yet it becomes desperate, and he will rather hazard his life than give up all thus. (1.) How he takes advice of his privy-council, who encourage him to stand it out. He speaks but poorly (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.7">v. 7</reference>), appeals to them whether Ben-hadad be not an unreasonable enemy, and do not seek mischief. What else could he expect from one who, without any provocation given him, had invaded his country and besieged his capital city? He owns to them how he had truckled to him before, and will have them advise him what he should do in this strait; and they speak bravely (<hi type="italic">Hearken not to him, nor consent,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.8">v. 8</reference>), promising no doubt to stand by him in the refusal. (2.) Yet he expresses himself very modestly in his denial, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.9">v. 9</reference>. He owns Ben-hadad's dominion over him: "<hi type="italic">Tell my lord the king</hi> I have no design to affront him, nor to receded from the surrender I have already made; what I offered at first I will stand to, <hi type="italic">but this thing I may not do;</hi> I must not give what is none of my own." It was a mortification to Ben-hadad that even such an abject spirit as Ahab's durst deny him; yet it should seem, by his manner of expressing himself, that he durst not have done it if his people had not animated him. <div eID="gen6977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6978" type="x-p"/> 5. Ben-hadad proudly swears the ruin of Samaria. The threatening waves of his wrath, meeting with this check, rage and foam, and make a noise. In his fury, he imprecates the impotent revenge of his gods, <hi type="italic">if the dust of Samaria serve for handfuls for his army</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.10">v. 10</reference>), so numerous, so resolute, an army will be bring into the field against Samaria, and so confident is he of their success; it will be done as easily as the taking up of a handful of dust; all shall be carried away, even the ground on which the city stands. Thus confident is his pride, thus cruel is his malice; this prepares him to be ruined, though such a prince and such a people are unworthy of the satisfaction of seeing him ruined. <div eID="gen6978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6979" type="x-p"/> 6. Ahab sends him a decent rebuke to his assurance, dares not defy his menaces, only reminds him of the uncertain turns of war (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.11">v. 11</reference>): "Let not him that begins a war, and is girding on his sword, his armour, his harness, boast of victory, or think himself sure of it, <hi type="italic">as if he had put it off,</hi> and had come home a conqueror." This was one of the wisest words that ever Ahab spoke, and is a good item or momento to us all; it is folly to boast beforehand of any day, since we know not what it may bring forth (<reference osisRef="Prov.27.1">Prov. xxvii. 1</reference>), but especially to boast of a day of battle, which may prove as much against us as we promise ourselves it will be for us. It is impolitic to despise an enemy, and to be too sure of victory is the way to be beaten. Apply it to our spiritual conflicts. Peter fell by his confidence. While we are here we are but girding on the harness, and therefore must never boast as though we had put it off. <hi type="italic">Happy is the man that feareth always,</hi> and is never off his watch.
entries.d080e2fad41d29d84a8bd3776cc47ff8c046aa72: <div eID="gen6979" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Ben-hadad's Defeat. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 900.)</title> <div sID="gen6980" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> And it came to pass, when <hi type="italic">Benhadad</hi> heard this message, as he <hi type="italic">was</hi> drinking, he and the kings in the pavilions, that he said unto his servants, Set <hi type="italic">yourselves in array.</hi> And they set <hi type="italic">themselves in array</hi> against the city. <hi type="super">13</hi> And, behold, there came a prophet unto Ahab king of Israel, saying, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , Hast thou seen all this great multitude? behold, I will deliver it into thine hand this day; and thou shalt know that I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">14</hi> And Ahab said, By whom? And he said, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , <hi type="italic">Even</hi> by the young men of the princes of the provinces. Then he said, Who shall order the battle? And he answered, Thou. <hi type="super">15</hi> Then he numbered the young men of the princes of the provinces, and they were two hundred and thirty two: and after them he numbered all the people, <hi type="italic">even</hi> all the children of Israel, <hi type="italic">being</hi> seven thousand. <hi type="super">16</hi> And they went out at noon. But Benhadad <hi type="italic">was</hi> drinking himself drunk in the pavilions, he and the kings, the thirty and two kings that helped him. <hi type="super">17</hi> And the young men of the princes of the provinces went out first; and Benhadad sent out, and they told him, saying, There are men come out of Samaria. <hi type="super">18</hi> And he said, Whether they be come out for peace, take them alive; or whether they be come out for war, take them alive. <hi type="super">19</hi> So these young men of the princes of the provinces came out of the city, and the army which followed them. <hi type="super">20</hi> And they slew every one his man: and the Syrians fled; and Israel pursued them: and Benhadad the king of Syria escaped on an horse with the horsemen. <hi type="super">21</hi> And the king of Israel went out, and smote the horses and chariots, and slew the Syrians with a great slaughter. <div eID="gen6980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6981" type="x-p"/> The treaty between the besiegers and the besieged being broken off abruptly, we have here an account of the battle that ensued immediately. <div eID="gen6981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6982" type="x-p"/> I. The Syrians, the besiegers, had their directions from a drunken king, who gave orders over his cups, as he was <hi type="italic">drinking</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.12">v. 12</reference>), <hi type="italic">drinking himself drunk</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.16">v. 16</reference>) <hi type="italic">with the kings in the pavilions,</hi> and this at noon. Drunkenness is a sin which armies and their officers have of old been addicted to. Say not thou then that the former days were, in this respect, better than these, though these are bad enough. Had he not been very secure he would not have sat to drink; and, had he not been intoxicated, he would not have been so very secure. Security and sensuality went together in the old world, and Sodom, <reference osisRef="Luke.17.26-Luke.17.29">Luke xvii. 26</reference>, &c. Ben-hadad's drunkenness was the forerunner of his fall, as Belshazzar's was, <reference osisRef="Dan.5.1-Dan.5.31">Dan v</reference>. How could he prosper that preferred his pleasure before his business, and kept his kings to drink with him when they should have been at their respective posts to fight for him? In his drink, 1. He orders the town to be invested, the engines fixed, and every thing got ready for the making of a general attack (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.12">v. 12</reference>), but stirs not from his drunken club to see it done. <hi type="italic">Woe unto thee, O land! when thy king is</hi> such <hi type="italic">a child.</hi> 2. When the besieged made a sally (and, by that time, he was far gone) he gave orders to take them alive (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.18">v. 18</reference>), not to kill them, which might have been done more easily and safely, but to seize them, which gave them an opportunity of killing the aggressors; so imprudent was he in the orders he gave, as well as unjust, in ordering them to be taken prisoners though they came for peace and to renew the treaty. Thus, as is usual, he drinks, and forgets the law, both the policies and the justice of war. <div eID="gen6982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6983" type="x-p"/> II. The Israelites, the besieged, had their directions from an inspired prophet, one of the prophets of the Lord, whom Ahab had hated and persecuted: <hi type="italic">And behold a prophet, even one, drew near to the king of Israel;</hi> so it may be read, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.13">v. 13</reference>. <div eID="gen6983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6984" type="x-p"/> 1. Behold, and wonder, that God should send a prophet with a kind and gracious message to so wicked a prince as Ahab was; but he did it, (1.) For his people Israel's sake, who, though wickedly degenerated, were the seed of Abraham his friend and Jacob his chosen, the children of the covenant, and not yet cast off. (2.) That he might magnify his mercy, in doing good to one so evil and unthankful, might either bring him to repentance or leave him the more inexcusable. (3.) That he might mortify the pride of Ben-hadad and check his insolence. Ahab's idolatry shall be punished hereafter, but Ben-hadad's haughtiness shall be chastised now; for God resists the proud, and is pleased to say that <hi type="italic">he fears the wrath of the enemy,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.32.26-Deut.32.27">Deut. xxxii. 26, 27</reference>. There was but one prophet perhaps to be had in Samaria, and he drew near with this message, intimating that he had been forced to keep at a distance. Ahab, in his prosperity, would not have borne the sight of him, but now he bids him welcome, when none of the prophets of the groves can give him any assistance. He enquired not for a prophet of the Lord, but God sent one to him unasked, for he waits to be gracious. <div eID="gen6984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6985" type="x-p"/> 2. Two things the prophet does:—(1.) He animates Ahab with an assurance of victory, which was more than all the elders of Israel could give him (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.8">v. 8</reference>), though they promised to stand by him. This prophet, who is not named (for he <hi type="italic">spoke in God's name</hi>), tells him from God that this very day the siege shall be raised, and the army of the Syrians routed, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.13">v. 13</reference>. When the prophet said, <hi type="italic">Thus saith the Lord,</hi> we may suppose Ahab began to tremble, expecting a message of wrath; but he is revived when it proves a gracious one. He is informed what use he ought to make of this blessed turn of affairs: "<hi type="italic">Thou shalt know that I am Jehovah,</hi> the sovereign Lord of all." God's foretelling a thing that was so very unlikely proved that it was his own doing. (2.) He instructs him what to do for the gaining of this victory. [1.] He must not stay till the enemy attacked him, but must sally out upon them and surprise them in their trenches. [2.] The persons employed must be the <hi type="italic">young men of the princes of the provinces,</hi> the pages, the footmen, who were few in number, only 232, utterly unacquainted with war, and the unlikeliest men that could be thought of for such a bold attempt; yet these must do it, these weak and foolish things must be instruments of confounding the wise and strong, that, while Ben-hadad's boasting is punished, Ahab's may be prevented and precluded, and the <hi type="italic">excellency of the power may appear to be of God.</hi> [3.] Ahab must himself so far testify his confidence in the word of God as to command in person, though, in the eye of reason, he exposed himself to the utmost danger by it. But it is fit that those who have the benefit of God's promises should enter upon them. Yet, [4.] He is allowed to make use of what other forces he has at hand, to follow the blow, when these young men have broken the ice. All he had in Samaria, or within call, were but 7000 men, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.15">v. 15</reference>. It is observable that it is the same number with theirs that had not <hi type="italic">bowed the knee to Baal</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.19.18">ch. xix. 18</reference>), though, it is likely, not the same men. <div eID="gen6985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6986" type="x-p"/> III. The issue was accordingly. The proud Syrians were beaten, and the poor despised Israelites were more than conquerors. The young men gave an alarm to the Syrians just at noon, at high dinner-time, supported by what little force they had, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.16">v. 16</reference>. Ben-hadad despised them at first (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.18">v. 18</reference>), but when they had, with unparalleled bravery and dexterity, <hi type="italic">slain every one his man,</hi> and so put the army into disorder, that proud man durst not face them, but mounted immediately, drunk as he was, and made the best of his way, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.20">v. 20</reference>. See how God <hi type="italic">takes away the spirit of princes,</hi> and makes himself <hi type="italic">terrible to the kings of the earth.</hi> Now where are the silver and gold he demanded of Ahab? Where are the handfuls of Samaria's dust? Those that are most secure are commonly least courageous. Ahab failed not to improve this advantage, but <hi type="italic">slew the Syrians with a great slaughter,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.21">v. 21</reference>. Note, God oftentimes makes one wicked man a scourge to another.
entries.b95338d5d17bdcb76757f9b8d812ddd7d9543f58: <div eID="gen6986" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Ahab's Folly Reproved. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 900.)</title> <div sID="gen6987" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> And the prophet came to the king of Israel, and said unto him, Go, strengthen thyself, and mark, and see what thou doest: for at the return of the year the king of Syria will come up against thee. <hi type="super">23</hi> And the servants of the king of Syria said unto him, Their gods <hi type="italic">are</hi> gods of the hills; therefore they were stronger than we; but let us fight against them in the plain, and surely we shall be stronger than they. <hi type="super">24</hi> And do this thing, Take the kings away, every man out of his place, and put captains in their rooms: <hi type="super">25</hi> And number thee an army, like the army that thou hast lost, horse for horse, and chariot for chariot: and we will fight against them in the plain, <hi type="italic">and</hi> surely we shall be stronger than they. And he hearkened unto their voice, and did so. <hi type="super">26</hi> And it came to pass at the return of the year, that Benhadad numbered the Syrians, and went up to Aphek, to fight against Israel. <hi type="super">27</hi> And the children of Israel were numbered, and were all present, and went against them: and the children of Israel pitched before them like two little flocks of kids; but the Syrians filled the country. <hi type="super">28</hi> And there came a man of God, and spake unto the king of Israel, and said, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , Because the Syrians have said, The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> God of the hills, but he <hi type="italic">is</hi> not God of the valleys, therefore will I deliver all this great multitude into thine hand, and ye shall know that I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">29</hi> And they pitched one over against the other seven days. And <hi type="italic">so</hi> it was, that in the seventh day the battle was joined: and the children of Israel slew of the Syrians a hundred thousand footmen in one day. <hi type="super">30</hi> But the rest fled to Aphek, into the city; and <hi type="italic">there</hi> a wall fell upon twenty and seven thousand of the men <hi type="italic">that were</hi> left. And Benhadad fled, and came into the city, into an inner chamber. <div eID="gen6987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6988" type="x-p"/> We have here an account of another successful campaign which Ahab, by divine aid, made against the Syrians, in which he gave them a greater defeat than in the former. Strange! Ahab idolatrous and yet victorious, a persecutor and yet a conqueror! God has wise and holy ends in suffering wicked men to prosper, and glorifies his own name thereby. <div eID="gen6988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6989" type="x-p"/> I. Ahab is admonished by a prophet to prepare for another war, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.22">v. 22</reference>. It should seem, he was now secure, and looked but a little way before him. Those that are careless of their souls are often as careless of their outwards affairs; but the prophet (to whom God made known the following counsels of the Syrians) told him they would renew their attempt at the return of the year, hoping to retrieve the honour they had lost and be avenged for the blow they had received. He therefore bade him strengthen himself, put himself into a posture of defence, and be ready to give them a warm reception. God had decreed the end, but Ahab must use the means, else he tempts God: "Help thyself, strengthen thyself, and God will help and strengthen thee." The enemies of God's Israel are restless in their malice, and, though they may take some breathing-time for themselves, yet they are still <hi type="italic">breathing out threatenings and slaughter</hi> against the church. It concerns us always to expect assaults from our spiritual enemies, and therefore to mark and see what we do. <div eID="gen6989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6990" type="x-p"/> II. Ben-hadad is advised by those about him concerning the operations of the next campaign. 1. They advised him to <hi type="italic">change his ground,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.23">v. 23</reference>. They took it for granted that it was not Israel, but Israel's gods, that beat them (so great a regard was then universally had to invisible powers); but they speak very ignorantly of Jehovah—that he was <hi type="italic">many,</hi> whereas he is one and his name one,—that he was <hi type="italic">their</hi> God only, a local deity, peculiar to that nation, whereas he is the Creator and ruler of all the world,—and that he was a God <hi type="italic">of the hills</hi> only, because David their great prophet had said, <hi type="italic">I will lift up my eyes to the hills whence cometh my help</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.121.1">Ps. cxxi. 1</reference>), and that <hi type="italic">his foundation was in the holy mountain</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.87.1">Ps. lxxxvii. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.78.54">lxxviii. 54</reference>), and much was said of his <hi type="italic">holy hill</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.15.1">Ps. xv. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.24.3">xxiv. 3</reference>); supposing him altogether such a one as their imaginary deities, they fancied he was confined to his hills, and could not or would not come down from them, and therefore an army in the valley would be below his cognizance and from under his protection. Thus vain were the <hi type="italic">Gentiles in their imaginations</hi> concerning God, so wretchedly were <hi type="italic">their foolish hearts darkened,</hi> and, <hi type="italic">professing themselves to be wise, they became fools.</hi> 2. They advised him to change his officers (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.24-1Kgs.20.25">v. 24, 25</reference>), not to employ the kings, who were commanders by birth, but captains rather, who were commanders by merit, who were inured to war, would not affect to make a show like the kings, but would go through with business. Let every man be employed in that which he is brought up to and used to, and preferred to that which he is fit for. Syria, it seems, was rich and populous, when it could furnish recruits sufficient, after so great a defeat, <hi type="italic">horse for horse, chariot for chariot.</hi> <div eID="gen6990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6991" type="x-p"/> III. Both armies take the field. Ben-hadad, with his Syrians, encamps near Aphek, in the tribe of Asher. It is probable that Asher was a city in his own possession, one of those which his father had won (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.34">v. 34</reference>), and the country about it was flat and level, and fit for his purpose, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.26">v. 26</reference>. Ahab, with his forces, posted himself at some distance over against them, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.27">v. 27</reference>. The disproportion of numbers was very remarkable. <hi type="italic">The children of Israel,</hi> who were cantoned in two battalions, looked like <hi type="italic">two little flocks of kids,</hi> their numbers small, their equipage mean, and the figure they made contemptible; <hi type="italic">but the Syrians filled the country</hi> with their numbers, their noise, their chariots, their carriages, and their baggage. <div eID="gen6991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6992" type="x-p"/> IV. Ahab is encouraged to fight the Syrians, notwithstanding their advantages and confidence. A man of God is sent to him, to tell him that this numerous army shall <hi type="italic">all be delivered into his hand</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.28">v. 28</reference>), but not for his sake; be it known to him, he is utterly unworthy for whom God will do this. God would not do it because Ahab had praised God or prayed to him (we do not read that he did either), but because the Syrians had blasphemed God, and had said, He is <hi type="italic">the God of the hills and not of the valleys;</hi> therefore God will do it in his own vindication, and to preserve the honour of his own name. If the Syrians had said, "Ahab and his people have forgotten their God, and so put themselves out of his protection, and therefore we may venture to attack them," God would probably have delivered Israel into their hands; but when they go upon a presumption so very injurious to the divine omnipotence, and the honour of him who is Lord of all hosts, not only in hills and valleys, but in heaven and earth, which they are willingly ignorant of, they shall be undeceived, at the expense of that vast army which is so much their pride and confidence. <div eID="gen6992" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6993" type="x-p"/> V. After the armies had faced one another seven days (the Syrians, it is likely, boasting, and the Israelites trembling), they engaged, and the Syrians were totally routed, 100,000 men slain by the sword of Israel in the field of battle (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.29">v. 29</reference>), and 27,000 men, that thought themselves safe <hi type="italic">under the walls of Aphek,</hi> a fortified city (from the walls of which the shooters might annoy the enemy if they pursued them, <reference osisRef="2Sam.11.24">2 Sam. xi. 24</reference>), found their bane where they hoped for protection: the wall fell upon them, probably overthrown by an earthquake, and, the cities of Canaan being walled up to heaven, it reached a great way, and they were all killed, or hurt, or overwhelmed with dismay. Ben-hadad, who thought his city Aphek would hold out against the conquerors, finding it thus unwalled, and the remnant of his forces dispirited and dispersed, had nothing but secresy to rely upon for safety, and therefore hid himself in <hi type="italic">a chamber within a chamber,</hi> lest the pursuers should seize him. See how the greatest confidence often ends in the greatest cowardice. "Now is the God of Israel the <hi type="italic">God of the valleys</hi> or no?" He shall know now that he is forced <hi type="italic">into an inner chamber to hide himself,</hi> see <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.25">ch. xxii. 25</reference>.
entries.62fce864bc0030600f8310cf41c52dda17b06596: <div eID="gen6993" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6994" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">31</hi> And his servants said unto him, Behold now, we have heard that the kings of the house of Israel <hi type="italic">are</hi> merciful kings: let us, I pray thee, put sackcloth on our loins, and ropes upon our heads, and go out to the king of Israel: peradventure he will save thy life. <hi type="super">32</hi> So they girded sackcloth on their loins, and <hi type="italic">put</hi> ropes on their heads, and came to the king of Israel, and said, Thy servant Benhadad saith, I pray thee, let me live. And he said, <hi type="italic">Is</hi> he yet alive? he <hi type="italic">is</hi> my brother. <hi type="super">33</hi> Now the men did diligently observe whether <hi type="italic">any thing would come</hi> from him, and did hastily catch <hi type="italic">it:</hi> and they said, Thy brother Benhadad. Then he said, Go ye, bring him. Then Benhadad came forth to him; and he caused him to come up into the chariot. <hi type="super">34</hi> And <hi type="italic">Benhadad</hi> said unto him, The cities, which my father took from thy father, I will restore; and thou shalt make streets for thee in Damascus, as my father made in Samaria. Then <hi type="italic">said Ahab,</hi> I will send thee away with this covenant. So he made a covenant with him, and sent him away. <hi type="super">35</hi> And a certain man of the sons of the prophets said unto his neighbour in the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , Smite me, I pray thee. And the man refused to smite him. <hi type="super">36</hi> Then said he unto him, Because thou hast not obeyed the voice of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , behold, as soon as thou art departed from me, a lion shall slay thee. And as soon as he was departed from him, a lion found him, and slew him. <hi type="super">37</hi> Then he found another man, and said, Smite me, I pray thee. And the man smote him, so that in smiting he wounded <hi type="italic">him.</hi> <hi type="super">38</hi> So the prophet departed, and waited for the king by the way, and disguised himself with ashes upon his face. <hi type="super">39</hi> And as the king passed by, he cried unto the king: and he said, Thy servant went out into the midst of the battle; and, behold, a man turned aside, and brought a man unto me, and said, Keep this man: if by any means he be missing, then shall thy life be for his life, or else thou shalt pay a talent of silver. <hi type="super">40</hi> And as thy servant was busy here and there, he was gone. And the king of Israel said unto him, So <hi type="italic">shall</hi> thy judgment <hi type="italic">be;</hi> thyself hast decided <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <hi type="super">41</hi> And he hasted, and took the ashes away from his face; and the king of Israel discerned him that he <hi type="italic">was</hi> of the prophets. <hi type="super">42</hi> And he said unto him, Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , Because thou hast let go out of <hi type="italic">thy</hi> hand a man whom I appointed to utter destruction, therefore thy life shall go for his life, and thy people for his people. <hi type="super">43</hi> And the king of Israel went to his house heavy and displeased, and came to Samaria. <div eID="gen6994" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6995" type="x-p"/> Here is an account of what followed upon the victory which Israel obtained over the Syrians. <div eID="gen6995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6996" type="x-p"/> I. Ben-hadad's tame and mean submission. Even in his inner chamber he feared, and would, if he could, flee further, though none pursued. His servants, seeing him and themselves reduced to the last extremity, advised that they should surrender at discretion, and make themselves prisoners and petitioners to Ahab for their lives, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.31">v. 31</reference>. The servants will put their lives in their hands, and venture first, and their master will act according as they speed. Their inducement to take this course is the great reputation the kings of Israel had for clemency above any of their neighbours: "We have heard that they are merciful kings, not oppressive to their subjects that are under their power" (as governments then went, that of Israel was one of the most easy and gentle), "and therefore not cruel to their enemies when they lie at their mercy." Perhaps they had this notion of the kings of Israel because they had heard that the God of Israel proclaimed his name <hi type="italic">gracious and merciful,</hi> and they concluded their kings would make their God their pattern. It was an honour to the kings of Israel to be thus represented, as indeed every Israelite is then dressed as becomes him when he <hi type="italic">puts on bowels of mercies.</hi> "They are merciful kings, therefore we may hope to find mercy upon our submission." This encouragement poor sinners have to repent and humble themselves before God. "Have we not heard that the God of Israel is a merciful God? Have we not found him so? Let us therefore rend our hearts and return to him." <reference osisRef="Joel.2.13">Joel ii. 13</reference>. That is evangelical repentance which flows from an apprehension of the mercy of God in Christ; <hi type="italic">there is forgiveness with him.</hi> Two things Ben-hadad's servants undertake to represent to Ahab:—1. Their master a penitent; for they <hi type="italic">girded sackcloth on their loins,</hi> as mourners, and <hi type="italic">put ropes on their heads,</hi> as condemned criminals going to execution, pretending to be sorry that they had invaded his country and disturbed his repose, and owning that they deserved to be hanged for it. Here they are ready to do penance for it, and throw themselves at the feet of him whom they had injured. Many pretend to repent of their wrong-doing, when it does not succeed, who, if they had prospered in it, would have justified it and gloried in it. 2. Their master a beggar, a beggar for his life: <hi type="italic">Thy servant Ben-hadad saith, "I pray thee, let me live,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.32">v. 32</reference>. Though I live a perpetual exile from my own country, and captive in this, yet, upon any terms, <hi type="italic">let me live.</hi>" What a great change is here, (1.) In his condition! How has he fallen from the height of power and prosperity to the depths of disgrace and distress, and all the miseries of poverty and slavery! See the uncertainty of human affairs; such turns are they subject to that the spoke which was uppermost may soon come to be undermost. (2.) In his temper—in the beginning of the chapter hectoring, swearing, and threatening, and none more high in his demands, but here crouching and whining and none more low in his requests! How meanly does he beg his life at the hand of him upon whom he had there been trampling! The most haughty in prosperity are commonly most abject in adversity: an even spirit will be the same in both conditions. See how God glorified himself when he <hi type="italic">looks upon proud men and abases them, and hides them in the dust together,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.40.11-Job.40.13">Job xl. 11-13</reference>. <div eID="gen6996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6997" type="x-p"/> II. Ahab's foolish acceptance of his submission, and the league he suddenly made with him upon it. He was proud to be thus courted by him whom he had feared, and enquired for him with great tenderness: <hi type="italic">Is he yet alive? He is my brother,</hi> brother-king, though not brother-Israelite: and Ahab valued himself more upon his royalty than on his religion, and others accordingly. "<hi type="italic">Is he thy brother, Ahab?</hi> Did he use thee like a brother when he sent thee that barbarous message? <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.5-1Kgs.20.6">v. 5, 6</reference>. Would he have called thee brother if he had been the conqueror? Would he now have called himself <hi type="italic">thy servant</hi> if he had not been reduced to the utmost strait? Canst thou suffer thyself to be thus imposed upon by a forced and counterfeit submission?" This word <hi type="italic">brother</hi> they caught at (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.33">v. 33</reference>), and were thereby encouraged to go and fetch him to the king. He that calls him <hi type="italic">brother</hi> will let him live. Let poor penitents hear God, in his word, calling them <hi type="italic">children</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.31.20">Jer. xxxi. 20</reference>), catch at it, echo to it, and call him <hi type="italic">Father.</hi> Ben-hadad, upon his submission, shall not only be honourably conveyed (he <hi type="italic">took him up into the chariot</hi>), but treated with as an ally (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.34">v. 34</reference>): he <hi type="italic">made a covenant with him,</hi> not consulting God's prophets, or the elders of the land, or himself, concerning what was fit to be insisted on, but, as if Ben-hadad had been conqueror, he shall make his own terms. He might now have demanded some of Ben-hadad's cities, when all of them lay at the mercy of his victorious army; but was content with the restitution of his own. He might now have demanded the stores, and treasures, and magazines of Damascus, to augment the wealth and strength of his own kingdom, but was content with a poor liberty, at his own expense, to build streets there, a point of honour and no advantage, or no more than what the kings of Syria had had in Samaria, though they had never had so much power as he had now to support the demand of it. With this covenant he sent him away, without so much as reproving him for his blasphemous reflections upon the God of Israel, for whose honour Ahab had no concern. Note, There are those on whom success is ill bestowed; they know not how to serve God, or their generation, or even their own true interests, with their prosperity. <hi type="italic">Let favour be shown to the wicked, yet will he not learn righteousness.</hi> <div eID="gen6997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6998" type="x-p"/> III. The reproof given to Ahab for his clemency to Ben-hadad and his covenant with him. It was given him by a prophet, in the name of the Lord, the Jews say by Micaiah, and not unlikely, for Ahab complains of him (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.8">ch. xxii. 8</reference>) that he used to <hi type="italic">prophesy evil concerning him.</hi> This prophet designed to reprove Ahab by a parable, that he might oblige him to condemn himself, as Nathan and the woman of Tekoa did David. To make his parable the more plausible, he finds it necessary to put himself into the posture of a wounded soldier. 1. With some difficulty he gets himself wounded, for he would not wound himself with his own hands. He commanded one of his brother prophets, his <hi type="italic">neighbour,</hi> or <hi type="italic">companion</hi> (for so the word signifies), to smite him, and this in God's name (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.35">v. 35</reference>), but finds him not so willing to give the blow as he is to receive it; he refused to smite him: others, he thought, were forward enough to smite prophets, they need not smite one another. We cannot but think it was from a good principle he declined it. "If it must be done, let another do it, not I; I cannot find it in my heart to strike my friend." Good men can much more easily receive a wrongful blow than give one; yet because he disobeyed an express command of God (which was so much the worse if he was himself a prophet), like that other disobedient prophet (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.13.24">ch. xiii. 24</reference>), he was presently <hi type="italic">slain by a lion,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.36">v. 36</reference>. This was intended, not only to show, in general, how provoking disobedience is (<reference osisRef="Col.3.6">Col. iii. 6</reference>), but to intimate to Ahab (who no doubt was told the story) that if a good prophet were thus punished for sparing his friend and God's, when God said, <hi type="italic">Smite,</hi> of much sorer punishment should a wicked king be thought worthy, who spared his enemy and God's, when God said, <hi type="italic">Smite. Shall mortal man</hi> pretend to <hi type="italic">be more just than God, more pure</hi> or more compassionate <hi type="italic">than his Maker?</hi> We must be merciful as he is merciful, and not otherwise. The next he met with made no difficulty of smiting him (<hi type="italic">Volentinon fit injuria</hi>—<hi type="italic">He that asks for an injury is not wronged by it</hi>) and did it so that he <hi type="italic">wounded him,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.37">v. 37</reference>. He fetched blood with the blow, probably in his face. 2. Wounded as he was, and disguised with ashes that he might not be known to be a prophet, he made his application to the king in a story wherein he charged himself with such a crime as the king was now guilty of in sparing Ben-hadad, and waited for the king's judgment upon it. The case in short is this—A prisoner taken in the battle was committed to his custody by a man (we may suppose one that had authority over him as his superior officer) with this charge, <hi type="italic">If he be missing, thy life shall be for his life,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.39">v. 39</reference>. The prisoner has made his escape through his carelessness. Can the chancery in the king's breast relieve him against his captain, who demands his life in lieu of the prisoner's? "By no means," says the king, "thou shouldst either not have undertaken the trust or been more careful and faithful to it; there is no remedy (<hi type="italic">Currat lex</hi>—<hi type="italic">Let the law take its course</hi>), thou hast forfeited thy bond, and execution must go out upon it: <hi type="italic">So shall thy doom be, thou thyself hast decided it.</hi>" Now the prophet has what he would have, puts off his disguise, and is known by Ahab himself to be a prophet (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.41">v. 41</reference>) and plainly tells him, "<hi type="italic">Thou art the man.</hi> Is it <hi type="italic">my</hi> doom? No, it is <hi type="italic">thine; thou thyself hast decided it.</hi> Out of thy own mouth art thou judged. God, thy superior and commander-in-chief, delivered into thy hands one plainly marked for destruction both by his own pride and God's providence, and thou hast not carelessly lost him, but wittingly and willingly dismissed him, and so hast been false to thy trust, and lost the end of thy victory; expect therefore no other than that <hi type="italic">thy life shall go for his life,</hi> which thou hast spared" (and so it did, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.35">ch. xxii. 35</reference>), "and thy <hi type="italic">people for his people,</hi> whom likewise thou hast spared," and so they did afterwards, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.10.32-2Kgs.10.33">2 Kings x. 32, 33</reference>. When their other sins brought them low, this came into the account. There is a time when <hi type="italic">keeping back the sword from blood</hi> is <hi type="italic">doing the work of the Lord deceitfully,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.48.10">Jer. xlviii. 10</reference>. Foolish pity spoils the city. 3. We are told how Ahab resented this reproof. He <hi type="italic">went to his house heavy and displeased</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.43">v. 43</reference>), not truly penitent, or seeking to undo what he had done amiss, but enraged at the prophet, exasperated against God (as if he had been too severe in the sentence passed upon him), and yet vexed at himself, every way out of humour, notwithstanding his victory. He who by his providence had mortified the pride of one king, by his word cast a damp upon the triumphs of another. <hi type="italic">Be wise therefore, O you kings! and be instructed to serve the Lord with fear and rejoice with trembling,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.2.10-Ps.2.11">Ps. ii. 10, 11</reference>.  <chapter eID="1Kgs.20"/> <div eID="gen6998" type="x-p"/>

entries.ccf733b45a35cb45b0b71a0c4d97736df2a61b97: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3298"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 20</title> <div sID="gen4627" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.1-1Kgs.20.12">1Ki 20:1-12</reference>. Ben-hadad Besieges Samaria.<div eID="gen4627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4628" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3298"/><hi type="bold">1. Ben-hadad the king of Syria--</hi>This monarch was the son of that Ben-hadad who, in the reign of Baasha, made a raid on the northern towns of Galilee (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.20">1Ki 15:20</reference>). The thirty-two kings that were confederate with him were probably tributary princes. The ancient kings of Syria and Phoenicia ruled only over a single city, and were independent of each other, except when one great city, as Damascus, acquired the ascendency, and even then they were allied only in time of war. The Syrian army encamped at the gates and besieged the town of Samaria. <div eID="gen4628" type="x-p"/>
entries.a3250e2ef49377e54255baa0f2a2bfbc9f1840c8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3299"/><div sID="gen4629" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3299"/><hi type="bold">2-12. Thus said Ben-hadad, Thy silver and thy gold is mine--</hi>To this message sent him during the siege, Ahab returned a tame and submissive answer, probably thinking it meant no more than an exaction of tribute. But the demand was repeated with greater insolence; and yet, from the abject character of Ahab, there is reason to believe he would have yielded to this arrogant claim also, had not the voice of his subjects been raised against it. Ben-hadad's object in these and other boastful menaces was to intimidate Ahab. But the weak sovereign began to show a little more spirit, as appears in his abandoning "my lord the king" for the single "tell him," and giving him a dry but sarcastic hint to glory no more till the victory is won. Kindling into a rage at the cool defiance, Ben-hadad gave orders for the immediate sack of the city. <div eID="gen4629" type="x-p"/>
entries.35006cd05f8bd62a53cb47d59d22df9d53eaf27e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3301"/><div sID="gen4633" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3301"/><hi type="bold">13-21. behold, there came a prophet unto Ahab--</hi>Though the king and people of Israel had highly offended Him, God had not utterly cast them off. He still cherished designs of mercy towards them, and here, though unasked, gave them a signal proof of His interest in them, by a prophet's animating announcement that the Lord would that day deliver the mighty hosts of the enemy into his hand by means of a small, feeble, inadequate band. Conformably to the prophet's instructions, two hundred thirty-two young men went boldly out towards the camp of the enemy, while seven thousand more, apparently volunteers, followed at some little distance, or posted themselves at the gate, to be ready to reinforce those in front if occasion required it. Ben-hadad and his vassals and princes were already, at that early hour--scarcely midday--deep in their cups; and though informed of this advancing company, yet confiding in his numbers, or it may be, excited with wine, he ordered with indifference the proud intruders to be taken alive, whether they came with peaceful or hostile intentions. It was more easily said than done; the young men smote right and left, making terrible havoc among their intended captors; and their attack, together with the sight of the seven thousand, who soon rushed forward to mingle in the fray, created a panic in the Syrian army, who immediately took up flight. Ben-hadad himself escaped the pursuit of the victors on a fleet horse, surrounded by a squadron of horse guards. This glorious victory, won so easily, and with such a paltry force opposed to overwhelming numbers, was granted that Ahab and his people might know (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.13">1Ki 20:13</reference>) that God is the Lord. But we do not read of this acknowledgment being made, or of any sacrifices being offered in token of their national gratitude. <div eID="gen4633" type="x-p"/>
entries.dc4ce002e6f5f6bff9db3ef326aba918ca3449bd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3302"/><div sID="gen4634" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3302"/><hi type="bold">22-26. the prophet came to the king of Israel, and said--</hi>The same prophet who had predicted the victory shortly reappeared, admonishing the king to take every precaution against a renewal of hostilities in the following campaign.<div eID="gen4634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4635" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">at the return of the year--</hi>that is, in spring, when, on the cessation of the rainy season, military campaigns (<reference osisRef="2Sam.11.1">2Sa 11:1</reference>), were anciently begun. It happened as the prophet had forewarned. Brooding over their late disastrous defeat, the attendants of Ben-hadad ascribed the misfortune to two causes--the one arose from the principles of heathenism which led them to consider the gods of Israel as "gods of the hills"; whereas their power to aid the Israelites would be gone if the battle was maintained on the plains. The other cause to which the Syrian courtiers traced their defeat at Samaria, was the presence of the tributary kings, who had probably been the first to take flight; and they recommended "captains to be put in their rooms." Approving of these recommendations, Ben-hadad renewed his invasion of Israel the next spring by the siege of Aphek in the valley of Jezreel (compare <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.1">1Sa 29:1</reference>, with <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.4">1Sa 28:4</reference>), not far from En-dor. <div eID="gen4635" type="x-p"/>
entries.0b5629b208afc64910f7f20ded1c96169d3f5396: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3303"/><div sID="gen4636" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3303"/><hi type="bold">27-31. like two little flocks of kids--</hi>Goats are never seen in large flocks, or scattered, like sheep; and hence the two small but compact divisions of the Israelite force are compared to goats, not sheep. Humanly speaking, that little handful of men would have been overpowered by numbers. But a prophet was sent to the small Israelite army to announce the victory, in order to convince the Syrians that the God of Israel was omnipotent everywhere, in the valley as well as on the hills. And, accordingly, after the two armies had pitched opposite each other for seven days, they came to an open battle. One hundred thousand Syrians lay dead on the field, while the fugitives took refuge in Aphek, and there, crowding on the city walls, they endeavored to make a stand against their pursuers; but the old walls giving way under the incumbent weight, fell and buried twenty-seven thousand in the ruins. Ben-hadad succeeded in extricating himself, and, with his attendants, sought concealment in the city, fleeing from chamber to chamber; or, as some think it, an inner chamber, that is, a harem; but seeing no ultimate means of escape, he was advised to throw himself on the tender mercies of the Israelitish monarch. <div eID="gen4636" type="x-p"/>
entries.ca4e61c213e6fdd5e78bd12ae60fec6e58f493a9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3304"/><div sID="gen4637" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3304"/><hi type="bold">32-34. put ropes on their heads--</hi>Captives were dragged by ropes round their necks in companies, as is depicted on the monuments of Egypt. Their voluntary attitude and language of submission flattered the pride of Ahab, who, little concerned about the dishonor done to the God of Israel by the Syrian king, and thinking of nothing but victory, paraded his clemency, called the vanquished king "his brother," invited him to sit in the royal chariot, and dismissed him with a covenant of peace. <div eID="gen4637" type="x-p"/>
entries.a64745f7315a5aa130eb80a33b64094a16bfc95a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3306"/><div sID="gen4640" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3306"/><hi type="bold">35-38. Smite me--</hi>This prophet is supposed (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.8">1Ki 20:8</reference>) to have been Micaiah. The refusal of his neighbor to smite the prophet was manifestly wrong, as it was a withholding of necessary aid to a prophet in the discharge of a duty to which he had been called by God, and it was severely punished [1Ki 20:36], as a beacon to warn others (see on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.13.2-1Kgs.13.24">1Ki 13:2-24</reference>). The prophet found a willing assistant, and then, waiting for Ahab, leads the king unconsciously, in the parabolic manner of Nathan (<reference osisRef="2Sam.12.1-2Sam.12.4">2Sa 12:1-4</reference>), to pronounce his own doom; and this consequent punishment was forthwith announced by a prophet (see on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.21.17">1Ki 21:17</reference>). <div eID="gen4640" type="x-p"/>
entries.aac256c641a2eb28f7d3162f5a30d0a48a6178bd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3307"/><div sID="gen4641" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3307"/><hi type="bold">39. a talent of silver--</hi>£342.  <chapter eID="1Kgs.20"/>

entries.5439648624361672cc3f0ddb5e4a264dc2f21cf6: <div eID="gen12251" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen12252" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen12253" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen12253" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen12252" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen12254" type="x-p"/> Ben-hadad, king of Syria, and thirty-two kings, besiege Samaria, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.1">1Kgs 20:1</reference>. He sends an insulting message to Ahab; and insists on pillaging the whole city, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.2-1Kgs.20.7">1Kgs 20:2-7</reference>. The elders of Israel counsel the king not to submit to such shameful conditions, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.8">1Kgs 20:8</reference>. He sends a refusal to Ben-hadad; who, being enraged, vows revenge, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.9-1Kgs.20.12">1Kgs 20:9-12</reference>. A prophet comes to Ahab, and promises him victory, and gives him directions how he should order the battle, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.13-1Kgs.20.19">1Kgs 20:13-19</reference>. The Syrians are discomfited, and Ben-hadad scarcely escapes, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.20">1Kgs 20:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.21">1Kgs 20:21</reference>. The prophet warns Ahab to be on his guard, for the Syrians would return next year, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.22">1Kgs 20:22</reference>. The counsellors of the king of Syria instruct him how he may successfully invade Israel, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.23-1Kgs.20.25">1Kgs 20:23-25</reference>. He leads an immense army to Aphek, to fight with Ahab, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.26">1Kgs 20:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.27">1Kgs 20:27</reference>. A man of God encourages Ahab, who attacks the Syrians, and kills one hundred thousand of them, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.28">1Kgs 20:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.29">1Kgs 20:29</reference>. They retreat to Aphek, where twenty-seven thousand of them are slain by a casualty, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.30">1Kgs 20:30</reference>. Ben-hadad and his courtiers, being closely besieged in Aphek, and unable to escape, surrender themselves with sackcloth on their loins, and halters on their heads; the king of Israel receives them in a friendly manner, and makes a covenant with Ben-hadad, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.31-1Kgs.20.34">1Kgs 20:31-34</reference>. A prophet, by a symbolical action, shows him the impolicy of his conduct in permitting Ben-hadad to escape, and predicts his death and the slaughter of Israel, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.35-1Kgs.20.43">1Kgs 20:35-43</reference>. <div eID="gen12254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12255" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen12255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12256" type="x-p"/> Ben-hadad - Several MSS., and some early printed editions, have Ben-hadar, or the son of Hadar, as the Septuagint. He is supposed to be the same whom Asa stirred up against the king of Israel, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.18">1Kgs 15:18</reference>; or, as others, his son or grandson. <div eID="gen12256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12257" type="x-p"/> Thirty and two kings - Tributary chieftains of Syria and the adjacent countries. In former times every town and city had its independent chieftain. Both the Septuagint and Josephus place this war after the history of Naboth.
entries.581849feb14de7257d9afb51489a173ac32daa34: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen12257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12258" type="x-p"/> I am thine, and all that I have - He probably hoped by this humiliation to soften this barbarous king, and perhaps to get better conditions.
entries.1257fe2f43bbd18b12cff85d343e28946e519e59: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen12258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12259" type="x-p"/> Whatsoever is pleasant in thine eyes - It is not easy to discern in what this second requisition differed from the first; for surely his silver, gold, wives, and children, were among his most pleasant or desirable things. Jarchi supposes that it was the book of the law of the Lord which Ben-hadad meant, and of which he intended to deprive Israel. It is however evident that Ben-hadad meant to sack the whole city, and after having taken the royal treasures and the wives and children of the king, to deliver up the whole to be pillaged by his soldiers.
entries.f7a328935d8f410bd1f50b2dd414a6136d45724c: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen12259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12260" type="x-p"/> Hearken not unto him - The elders had every thing at stake, and they chose rather to make a desperate defense than tamely to yield to such degrading and ruinous conditions.
entries.ca53c3ebe0a7eebd4a3beff6dfef167080cf986c: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen12260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12261" type="x-p"/> If the dust of Samaria shall suffice - This is variously understood. Jonathan translates thus: "If the dust of Shomeron shall be sufficient for the soles of the feet of the people that shall accompany me;" i.e., I shall bring such an army that there will scarcely be room for them to stand in Samaria and its vicinity.
entries.054f1af9677950bcc511e9e1c6807757e1e41832: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen12261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12262" type="x-p"/> Let not him that girdeth on - This was no doubt a proverbial mode of expression. Jonathan translates, "Tell him, Let not him who girds himself and goes down to the battle, boast as he who has conquered and returned from it.
entries.740d433491d42ee82c86b149821260e3090327aa: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen12262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12263" type="x-p"/> In the pavilions - This word comes from papilio, a butterfly, because tents, when pitched or spread out, resembled such animals; partly because of the mode of their expansion, and partly because of the manner in which they were painted. <div eID="gen12263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12264" type="x-p"/> Set yourselves in array - The original word, שימו simu, which we translate by this long periphrasis, is probably a military term for Begin the attack, Invest the city, Every man to his post, or some such like expression.
entries.87eb6543b0192442322481b79ab3232a34ef4024: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen12264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12265" type="x-p"/> There came a prophet - Who this was we cannot tell; Jarchi says it was Micaiah, son of Imlah. It is strange that on such an occasion we hear nothing of Elijah or Elisha. Is it not possible that this was one of them disguised?
entries.8c8de48fd31e3874637437e7faff7349a0c184a5: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen12265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12266" type="x-p"/> By the young men of the princes of the provinces - These were probably some chosen persons out of the militia of different districts, raised by the princes of the provinces; the same as we would call lord-lieutenants of counties.
entries.1c41dc6869d94214dbee50b5d847294022da7c7a: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen12266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12267" type="x-p"/> Two hundred and thirty-two - These were probably the king's life or body guards; not all the militia, but two hundred and thirty of them who constituted the royal guard in Samaria. They were therefore the king's own regiment, and he is commanded by the prophet to put himself at their head. <div eID="gen12267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12268" type="x-p"/> Seven thousand - How low must the state of Israel have been at this time! These Jarchi thinks were the seven thousand who had not bowed the knee to Baal.
entries.ef39685491158b97784c26402886f65f411e5771: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen12268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12269" type="x-p"/> Take them alive - He was confident of victory. Do not slay them; bring them to me, they may give us some useful information.
entries.ececc233221ed3b418f00ee8d2830ee1e7c17819: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen12269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12270" type="x-p"/> The Syrians fled - They were doubtless panic-struck.
entries.e22dedb81fd4b5cd9169f5b834ff2a7f60526682: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen12270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12271" type="x-p"/> Their gods are gods of the hills - It is very likely that the small Israelitish army availed itself of the heights and uneven ground, that they might fight with greater advantage against the Syrian cavalry, for Ben-hadad came up against Samaria with horses and chariots, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.1">1Kgs 20:1</reference>. These therefore must be soon thrown into confusion when charging in such circumstances; indeed, the chariots must be nearly useless. <div eID="gen12271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12272" type="x-p"/> Let us fight against them in the plain - There our horses and chariots will all be able to bear on the enemy, and there their gods, whose influence is confined to the hills, will not be able to help them. It was a general belief in the heathen world that each district had its tutelary and protecting deity, who could do nothing out of his own sphere.
entries.95491dec2275857144ed098c65de73bd9d308762: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen12272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12273" type="x-p"/> Take the kings away - These were not acquainted with military affairs, or they had not competent skill. Put experienced captains in their place, and fight not but on the plains, and you will be sure of victory.
entries.bf7cce2fd7f016f492875b8e3840ef7a5e6b17ed: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen12273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12274" type="x-p"/> Ben-hadad numbered the Syrians, and went up to Aphek - There were several towns of this name; see the notes on <reference osisRef="Jos.12.18">Jos 12:18</reference>. It is supposed that the town mentioned here was situated in Libanus, upon the river Adonis, between Heliopolis and Biblos.
entries.b725d0f5f8f4752fbe11ff6c0bb0730645342c41: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen12274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12275" type="x-p"/> Because the Syrians have said - God resents their blasphemy, and is determined to punish it. They shall now be discomfited in such a way as to show that God's power is every where, and that the multitude of a host is nothing against him.
entries.3eebae22c447a4c13761f2cd622a39dd817550b7: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen12275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12276" type="x-p"/> Slew a hundred thousand footmen in one day - This number is enormous; but the MSS. and versions give no various reading.
entries.207e7d90989db3352fb5ffd1465c2f37ca6f6e34: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen12276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12277" type="x-p"/> A wall fell upon twenty and seven thousand - From the first view of this text it would appear that when the Syrians fled to Aphek, and shut themselves within the walls, the Israelites immediately brought all hands, and sapped the walls, in consequence of which a large portion fell, and buried twenty-seven thousand men. But perhaps the hand of God was more immediately in this disaster; probably a burning wind is meant. See at the end of the chapter, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.43">1Kgs 20:43</reference> (note). <div eID="gen12277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12278" type="x-p"/> Came into the city, into an inner chamber - However the passage above may be understood, the city was now, in effect, taken; and Ben-hadad either betook himself with his few followers to the citadel or to some secret hiding-place, where he held the council with his servants immediately mentioned.
entries.e31a2e282a65001c0909991b846d2dea71089d59: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen12278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12279" type="x-p"/> Put sackcloth on our loins, and ropes upon our heads - Let us show ourselves humbled in the deepest manner, and let us put ropes about our necks, and go submitting to his mercy, and deprecating his wrath. The citizens of Calais are reported to have acted nearly in the same way when they surrendered their city to Edward III., king of England, in 1346. See at the end, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.43">1Kgs 20:43</reference> (note).
entries.c6baa8d82e99de5610b3e1b7fca6db4b4787d0c3: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen12279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12280" type="x-p"/> Thy servant Ben-hadad - See the vicissitude of human affairs! A little before he was the haughtiest of all tyrants, and Ahab calls him his lord; now, so much is he humbled, that he will be glad to be reputed Ahab's slave!
entries.edb39997b10f370e334d180aa23806baab3d9838: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen12280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12281" type="x-p"/> Did hastily catch it - They were watching to see if any kind word should be spoken by him, from which they might draw a favorable omen; and when they heard him use the word brother, it gave them much encouragement.
entries.9f5ca368281ab9fbe9424ec3afd0a0388bc89bf4: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen12281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12282" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt make streets for thee in Damascus - It appears that it was customary for foreigners to have a place assigned to them, particularly in maritime towns, where they might deposit and vend their merchandise. This was the very origin of European settlements in Asiatic countries: "The people gave an inch to those strangers; and in consequence they took an ell." Under the pretense of strengthening the place where they kept their wares, to prevent depredations, they built forts, and soon gave laws to their entertainers. In vain did the natives wish them away; they had got power, and would retain it; and at last subjected these countries to their own dominion. <div eID="gen12282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12283" type="x-p"/> It was customary also, in the time of the crusades, to give those nations which were engaged in them streets, churches, and post dues, in those places which they assisted to conquer. The Genoese and Venetians had each a street in Accon, or St. Jean d'Acre, in which they had their own jurisdiction; with oven, mill, bagnio, weights, and measures. - See William of Tyre, and Harmer's Observations. <div eID="gen12283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12284" type="x-p"/> He made a covenant with him - According to the words recited above, putting him under no kind of disabilities whatsoever.
entries.521a5d29f4545eba78d06060cd6b9ba902fb2a84: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen12284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12285" type="x-p"/> In the word of the Lord - By the word or command of the Lord; that is, God has commanded thee to smite me. Refusing to do it, this man forfeited his life, as we are informed in the next verse. <div eID="gen12285" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12286" type="x-p"/> By this emblematical action he intended to inform Ahab that, as the man forfeited his life who refused to smite him when he had the Lord's command to do it; so he (Ahab) had forfeited his life, because he did not smite Ben-hadad when he had him in his power.
entries.a7afd00134dac0b6cac892f3b790bd45376c15f5: <hi type="bold">Verse 36</hi> <div eID="gen12286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12287" type="x-p"/> A lion found him, and slew him - This seems a hard measure, but there was ample reason for it. This person was also one of the sons of the prophets, and he knew that God frequently delivered his counsels in this way, and should have immediately obeyed; for the smiting could have had no evil in it when God commanded it, and it could be no outrage or injury to his fellow when he himself required him to do it.
entries.9eb8e9e68fc74df69f07d97826889c34b454b416: <hi type="bold">Verse 38</hi> <div eID="gen12287" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12288" type="x-p"/> Disguised himself with ashes upon his face - It does not immediately appear how putting ashes upon his face could disguise him. Instead of אפר apher, dust, Houbigant conjectures that it should be אפד aphad, a fillet or bandage. It is only the corner of the last letter which makes the difference; for the ד daleth and ר resh are nearly the same, only the shoulder of the former is square, the latter round. That bandage, not dust, was the original reading, seems pretty evident from its remains in two of the oldest versions, the Septuagint and the Chaldee; the former has Και κατεδησατο εν τελαμωνι τους οφθαλμους αυτου, "And he bound his eyes with a fillet." The latter has וכריך במעפריאעינוהי ukerich bemaaphira einohi; "And he covered his eyes with a cloth." The MSS. of Kennicott and De Rossi contain no various reading here; but bandage is undoubtedly the true one. However, in the way of mortification, both the Jews and Hindoos put ashes upon their heads and faces, and make themselves sufficiently disgusting.
entries.25177d4db122ddd0362728bb0e1360864ebd5908: <hi type="bold">Verse 39</hi> <div eID="gen12288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12289" type="x-p"/> Keep this man - The drift of this is at once seen; but Ahab, not knowing it, was led to pass sentence on himself.
entries.958c34dd966b6a777003795df49d86698fe5461e: <hi type="bold">Verse 41</hi> <div eID="gen12289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12290" type="x-p"/> Took the ashes away - He took the bandage from off his eyes: see on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.38">1Kgs 20:38</reference> (note). It was no doubt of thin cloth, through which he could see, while it served for a sufficient disguise.
entries.4e9438541609cb52211e43cf032d59cc6c2a3598: <hi type="bold">Verse 42</hi> <div eID="gen12290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12291" type="x-p"/> Thy life shall go for his life - This was fulfilled at the battle of Ramoth-gilead, where he was slain by the Syrians; see <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.34">1Kgs 22:34</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.35">1Kgs 22:35</reference>.
entries.c1d604c2350151b358746cb013ab50067fbbb076: <hi type="bold">Verse 43</hi> <div eID="gen12291" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12292" type="x-p"/> Heavy and displeased - Heavy or afflicted, because of these dreadful tidings; and displeased with the prophet for having announced them. Had he been displeased with himself, and humbled his soul before God, even those judgments, so circumstantially foretold, might have been averted. <div eID="gen12292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12293" type="x-p"/> 1. We have already seen, in <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.30">1Kgs 20:30</reference>, that according to our text, twenty-seven thousand men were slain by the falling of a wall. Serious doubts are entertained concerning the legitimacy of this rendering. I have, in the note, given the conjecture concerning sapping the foundation of the wall, and thus overthrowing them that were upon it. If instead of חומה chomah, a wall, we read חומה confusion or disorder, then the destruction of the twenty-seven thousand men may appear to have been occasioned by the disorganized state into which they fell; of which their enemies taking advantage, they might destroy the whole with ease. <div eID="gen12293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12294" type="x-p"/> But חומה chomah, a wall, becomes, as Dr. Kennicott has observed, a very different word when written without the ו vau, חמה which signifies heat; sometimes the sun, vehement heat, or the heat of the noon-day sun; and also the name of a wind, from its suffocating, parching quality. <div eID="gen12294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12295" type="x-p"/> The same noun, from יחם yacham, Dr. Castel explains by excandescentia, furor, venenum; burning, rage, poison. These renderings, says Dr. Kennicott, all concur to establish the sense of a burning wind, eminently blasting and destructive. I shall give a few instances from the Scripture: - We read in <reference osisRef="Job.27.21">Job 27:21</reference> : The east wind carrieth him away; where the word קדים kadim is καυσων, burning, in the Septuagint; and in the Vulgate, ventus urens, a burning wind. In <reference osisRef="Eze.19.12">Eze 19:12</reference> : She was plucked up בחמה she was cast down to the ground, and the east wind dried up her fruit; her strong rods were withered, and the fire consumed them. Hosea (<reference osisRef="Hos.13.15">Hos 13:15</reference>) mentions the desolation brought by an east wind, the wind of the Lord. What in <reference osisRef="Amo.4.9">Amo 4:9</reference> is, I have smitten you with blasting, in the Vulgate is, in vento vehemente, "with a vehement wind;" and in the Syriac, with a hot wind. <div eID="gen12295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12296" type="x-p"/> Let us apply these to the history: when Ben-hadad, king of Syria, was besieging Samaria the second time, the Israelites slew of the Syrians one hundred thousand footmen in one day; and it follows, that when the rest of the army fled to Aphek, twenty-seven thousand of the men that were left were suddenly destroyed by החומה hachomah, or החמה hachamah, a burning wind.
